newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends up on Calif. nuke outage.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends up on Calif. nuke outage.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures ended higher Monday on news of an unexpected two week outage at a California nuclear power facility, industry sources said.
Southern California Edison Co said Monday it expects the 1,070 megawatt (MW) San Onofre 2 nuclear unit in San Clemente, Calif., to remain off line until July 15 following a shutdown Sunday.
The unit was shut to replace its charge line check valves after scaling output back to 90 percent of capacity Thursday.
The adjoining San Onofre 3 nuclear unit, rated at 1,080 MW, remained in shut after being taken off line April 12 for refueling and was scheduled to resume operations near July 10.

The outage gave support to electricity futures and to short-term physical power prices. "It was quiet trade, and the higher numbers were all based on the California outage," said one Western electricity trader.

August Palo Verde (PV) ended up $2.64 at $34.90 per megawatt hour (MWh) following exchanges in a range of $33.30-35.10, while September finished up $1.00 at $28.71 following trades in a range of $28.25-29.00 per MWh.
Remaining PV deferreds finished between 20 and 50 cents higher.
August California Oregon Border (COB) closed down $1.03 at $23.40 per MWh after trades at $22.85-23.60, while September ended up $1.04 at $23.39 after exchanges in a range of $23.15-23.50 per MWh.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 689 PV and 272 COB contracts traded.

In the physical markets, peak firm COB electricity for Tuesday was quoted at $19.00-20.00 per MWh from $15.00-16.00 for Saturday and Monday. Firm, peak PV deliveries for Tuesday were quoted at $31.50-33.00, up sharply from $22.00-23.00 for Saturday/Monday deals.
The six to 10 day forecast called for temperatures in the Pacific Northwest to average below normal, while those in the Southwest would run above normal.
The WNP-2 nuclear plant in Washington state continued to await clearance from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission before beginning start-up operations.
Also, a 550 MW unit at the coal-fired Laramie River Station in Wyoming was said to have tripped off line Sunday, with no restart date available.

Seperately, late last week the Western Systems Coordinating Council board approved a derating of the Pacific Intertie transmission sytem to 6,300 MW from the current 7,200 MW, which was to be effective early Tuesday.
